findings.explanation: verifySignature() compares the X-Hub-Signature-256 HMAC (sig) against the locally computed HMAC (expected) using plain string equality (===) instead of crypto.timingSafeEqual. String === short-circuits on the first differing character, so response time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature are correct, letting a remote attacker recover the valid signature byte-by-byte via a timing side-channel and forge webhook payloads without knowing fbAppSecret.

The GET /webhook subscribe handshake compares the caller-supplied hub.verify_token against the configured fbVerifyToken secret with ===, not crypto.timingSafeEqual. Because === also short-circuits on the first mismatched character, an attacker probing this public endpoint can use response-time differences to brute-force fbVerifyToken character by character. Severity is lower than the signature check since this token only gates the one-time subscription handshake, not payload authenticity.
